Colorectal cancers are very common in developed areas such as the USA and western Europe, but rare among African and Asian populations. Genetic and di- etary factors are thought to be related to development of the disease.1 Inherited predisposition syndromes in- clude familial adenomatous polyposis and hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer.2,3 Most large bowel cancers arise within pre-existing intestinal polyps. Over 50% occur in the rectum and about 20% in the sigmoid colon. There may be direct invasion of neighbouring structures and metastatic spread to the lymph nodes, and to lungs, bone, and in particular, liver. Signs and symptoms include blood in the stools, altered bowel habit, anaemia, and weight loss; there may be local ob- struction (depending on location) or perforation. The first-line treatment for early-stage and locally- advanced disease (stages I to III; Dukes A to C) is sur- gery.4,5 Survival in early-stage disease is good: published 5-year overall survival rates are 80 to 95% in patients with stage I disease, but fall to 25 to 60% (depending on prog- nostic factors such as nodal involvement and degree of tu- mour invasiveness) in those with stage III disease.2 Adju- vant or neoadjuvant therapies have thus been widely investigated and incorporated into treatment.4,5 US guidelines for colon cancer4 consider adjuvant therapy unnecessary in stage I disease, but recommend adjuvant chemotherapy in most patients with resectable stage II or stage III disease. There is good evidence that fluorouracil-based adjuvant therapy improves survival in stage III disease,6-10 and it has been regarded as the standard of care.2,9,11,12 Recent results with the FOLFOX regimen (infusional fluorour- acil, folinic acid, and oxaliplatin) have suggested that it can improve disease-free (but not overall) survival
